title: Photo Sharing App
prompt: Design a mobile photo-sharing app: people upload photos, follow each other, scroll a feed of photos from accounts they follow, and like posts.

clarify.q: Is it photos only, or also video and multi-photo posts?
clarify.why: Video needs transcoding and adaptive streaming, a different pipeline. Photos only keeps processing to a resize job of a few hundred milliseconds.

clarify.q: Is the feed strictly newest-first from people I follow, or ranked?
clarify.why: Chronological lets us precompute a timeline per user. Ranking adds a scoring stage at read time and a candidate pool larger than one page.

clarify.q: How many daily users, and how many photos does a typical user post?
clarify.why: Upload rate sets storage growth, which is the biggest cost here. Feed opens set read QPS and CDN bandwidth.

clarify.q: Do we need to keep the full-resolution original forever?
clarify.why: Originals are ~83% of the bytes (2 of 2.4 MB). Keeping them in a cold storage class, or capping resolution at upload, changes cost by several times.

clarify.q: Are some accounts followed by tens of millions of people?
clarify.why: Celebrity accounts break write-time fan-out. Their existence decides whether we need a hybrid feed.

clarify.q: How fast must a new post show up in followers' feeds?
clarify.why: If a few seconds is fine, fan-out can be async through a queue. If it must be instant, the read path has to merge in fresh posts.

clarify.q: Are like counts allowed to be slightly behind?
clarify.why: Exact real-time counts on a viral post mean one hot row. Accepting a few seconds of lag lets us batch counter updates.

functional: A user uploads a photo with a caption; it appears on their profile.
Followers see the new post in their home feed, newest first, paged with a cursor.
Each photo is served in several sizes (thumbnail, feed, full screen) suited to the device.
A user can like and unlike a post; posts show a like count.
A user can follow and unfollow other accounts.
nonFunctional: Feed API p99 under 200 ms; first feed image visible under 1 s on 4G.
Uploaded photos are never lost: 11 nines durability for originals.
99.95% availability for feed reads; upload can degrade (queue and retry) before reads do.
New posts visible to followers within 10 s for normal accounts.
Like counts eventually consistent within a few seconds; a user always sees their own like immediately.
outOfScope: Ranking model, ads and recommendations to non-followers.
Direct messages, comments threading and search.
Content moderation models (we leave a hook for them in the pipeline).

assumptions: 50 M new photos per day (one in four users posts)
Original after client-side re-encode ≈ 2 MB; three derived sizes ≈ 0.4 MB together
Each user opens the feed 10 times a day and loads ~10 images per open
Average follower count 200; 5 likes per user per day

steps.label: Image egress
steps.math: 2 B opens × 10 images = 20 B/day ≈ 231 k/s; × 100 KB ≈ 23 GB/s ≈ 185 Gbps
steps.result: ≈ 185 Gbps average: only a CDN can serve this

steps.label: Fan-out writes
steps.math: 50 M posts × 200 followers = 10 B inserts/day ≈ 116 k/s

steps.label: Timeline cache
steps.math: 200 M users × 500 post IDs × 8 B = 800 GB
steps.result: ≈ 800 GB raw, ~1.6 TB with overhead: a Redis cluster

estimates.takeaway:
Bytes, not requests, dominate. Photo storage grows by ~44 PB a year and image egress is ~185 Gbps, so uploads go straight to object storage and reads come from a CDN. App servers never touch image bytes.

The metadata is small by comparison. 50 M rows a day at ~500 B is ~25 GB/day. The hard part of the request path is the feed: 23 k reads/s against 116 k fan-out inserts/s. That is why the timeline is precomputed in a cache and celebrity accounts are handled separately.

api.note: Returns a presigned PUT URL valid for 15 minutes. The client sends bytes directly to object storage, never through our servers.
Idempotency-Key header. 202 because thumbnails are generated async; the client shows its local copy meanwhile.

api.returns: 200 { items: [{ postId, author, caption, images: { thumb, feed, full }, likeCount, likedByMe }], nextCursor }
api.note: Cursor is an opaque (createdAt, postId) pair, so new posts do not shift pages.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so double taps and retries are safe.
Triggers a backfill of the followee's recent posts into the follower's timeline.

entities.name: Post
entities.why: Profile pages read one author's posts newest-first, so sharding by author keeps that a single-shard range scan on (authorId, postId desc).

entities.name: Follow
entities.why: Stored twice: 'who do I follow' and 'who follows me'. Fan-out reads the second one, and it can be millions of rows for a celebrity.

entities.name: Timeline
entities.why: Precomputed home feed, trimmed to the newest 500 IDs. Rebuildable from Post and Follow, so losing it is a latency problem, not data loss.

entities.name: Like
entities.why: One row per like makes like and unlike idempotent and answers 'did I like this'. The count lives in a separate counter fed by an event stream.

entities.name: Photo bytes
fields: standard class, cached at the edge
entities.why: Immutable, write-once blobs. Object keys never change, so CDN caches can use a one-year max-age.

data.note:
Metadata and bytes are split on purpose. Postgres holds what we query by; object storage holds what we only fetch by key. Post IDs embed a timestamp, so 'newest first' needs no extra index, and a cursor is just the last ID seen.

Likes go to Cassandra because the write rate (~12 k/s) and the hot-partition pattern suit a wide-row store. The displayed count is a separate counter (see deep dive) so a viral post does not mean 1 M writes to one row.

hld.summary:
The client asks the Upload service for a presigned URL and PUTs the photo straight into object storage. It then creates the post, which writes a row with status processing and emits a PostCreated event. Two independent consumers react: the image workers make three WebP sizes and flip the post to ready, and the fan-out workers push the post ID into each follower's Redis timeline.

On read, the Feed service takes the user's timeline IDs, merges in recent posts from the few celebrities they follow, hydrates post metadata from a cache, and returns CDN URLs. Image bytes only ever flow between object storage, the CDN and the phone. Likes write a row and an event, and a counter service applies counts in small batches.

diagram.title: Upload, processing and feed paths
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  App[Mobile app] -->|presigned PUT| OBJ["Object storage (originals)"]
  App --> GW[API gateway]
  GW --> PS[Post service]
  PS --> DB[(Posts DB)]
  PS --> BUS[Event bus]
  BUS --> IMG[Image workers]
  IMG --> OBJ2["Object storage (derived sizes)"]
  BUS --> FAN[Fan-out workers]
  FAN --> TL[(Timeline cache)]
  GW --> FEED[Feed service]
  FEED --> TL
  FEED --> DB
  App -->|GET image| CDN[CDN]
  CDN --> OBJ2

flows.title: Posting a photo
steps: App resizes to max 2048 px, computes a hash, and calls POST /v1/uploads to get a presigned URL.
App PUTs the bytes directly to object storage; a retry after a network drop simply re-PUTs to the same key.
App calls POST /v1/posts; the Post service writes the row (processing) and an outbox entry in one transaction.
Image workers consume PostCreated, generate thumb/feed/full WebP, write them, and mark the post ready.
Fan-out workers page through the author's followers and ZADD the post ID into each timeline, then ZREMRANGE to keep 500.

flows.title: Opening the home feed
steps: Feed service reads the top 20 IDs below the cursor from timeline:{userId}.
It fetches recent posts from followed celebrity accounts (pull side) and merges them by time.
It hydrates posts from a post cache (multi-get), dropping removed or still-processing ones.
It adds like counts and likedByMe, builds CDN URLs per size, and returns the page with nextCursor.
The app loads the feed-size image first and the full size only when the user taps.

flows.title: Liking a post
steps: PUT /like inserts (postId, userId) in Cassandra; if the row already existed nothing else happens.
A LikeChanged event (+1 or -1) goes to the bus.
The counter service sums events per post over ~1 s and applies one increment per post to the counter store.
The app shows the like optimistically, so the user never waits on the counter.

deepDives.title: Getting photo bytes into storage
deepDives.problem: At peak, ~1 750 uploads/s of ~2 MB each is ~3.5 GB/s of inbound bytes. Mobile networks drop mid-upload. If bytes pass through app servers, those servers become a bandwidth tier with long-held connections, and a deploy cuts every in-flight upload.

options.name: Upload through the API servers
options.how: Client POSTs multipart to our service, which streams to object storage.
pros: Simple auth and validation in one place
Can reject bad files before storing
cons: App fleet sized for 3.5 GB/s of bytes instead of for requests
Slow clients pin connections and threads
Every deploy breaks in-flight uploads

options.name: Presigned direct PUT to object storage
options.how: Server issues a short-lived URL scoped to one key, size and content type; the client PUTs there directly.
pros: Our servers handle only small JSON calls
Object storage absorbs bandwidth and scales on its own
Easy to retry: same URL, same key
cons: Validation happens after upload, in the image worker
Abandoned uploads leave orphans that need a lifecycle rule

options.name: Resumable chunked upload
options.how: Split into 5 MB parts (multipart upload); the client resumes from the last confirmed part.
pros: Survives flaky networks for big files
Parallel parts speed up large uploads
cons: More client and server state
Overkill for a 2 MB photo, which is one part anyway

deepDives.choice:
Presigned direct PUT. A 2 MB photo is one part, so chunking adds complexity for nothing. The post row only becomes ready after the image worker has decoded the file, checked size and type, and stripped EXIF location data, so a bad upload never reaches a feed. A lifecycle rule deletes originals with no post after 24 hours.

I would switch to resumable multipart if we add video or let users upload RAW files of 50 MB or more.

deepDives.title: Generating the derived sizes
deepDives.problem: Phones should not download a 2 MB original to show a 400 px tile. We need several sizes and a modern format. The question is when to make them: at upload, or when first requested.

options.name: Eager: resize at upload in an async worker
options.how: PostCreated triggers a worker that writes thumb (150 px), feed (1080 px) and full (2048 px) WebP files.
pros: Read path is pure static files, perfect for a CDN
Predictable cost: ~580 jobs/s, each a few hundred ms of CPU
cons: Adding a new size later means a backfill over billions of photos
Pays for sizes of photos that are never viewed

options.name: Lazy: resize on first request at the edge
options.how: CDN miss goes to a resize service that reads the original, resizes, and caches the result.
pros: New sizes and formats are free to add
No work for photos nobody views
cons: First viewer of each size waits ~300 ms extra
A viral post creates a thundering herd of misses on the resizer
Originals must stay in a fast storage class

options.name: Hybrid
options.how: Eagerly make the two sizes the feed always needs; generate rare sizes lazily.
pros: Feed path is always warm
Flexibility for new layouts
cons: Two code paths to run and monitor

deepDives.choice:
Hybrid. At ~580 uploads/s, eager resizing of thumb and feed sizes is cheap: about 580 × 0.3 s ≈ 175 CPU cores at average, under 600 at peak. Feed images are hit within minutes of posting, so lazy generation would only add latency for the first followers.

Odd sizes (a new tablet layout) go through the lazy resizer with request coalescing in front, so 1 000 simultaneous misses cause one resize. If storage cost became the main concern, I would go fully lazy and move originals to a cheaper tier.

deepDives.title: Building the home feed: push, pull or both
deepDives.problem: A feed read must return the newest posts from everyone the user follows in under 200 ms. Computing that on read means querying up to hundreds of authors per request at ~70 k requests/s. Precomputing on write means one post by an account with 50 M followers creates 50 M writes.

options.name: Fan-out on write (push)
options.how: When a post is created, insert its ID into every follower's timeline cache.
pros: Feed read is one cache lookup
Read latency independent of how many people you follow
cons: Celebrity posts cause millions of writes and minutes of delay
Work wasted on inactive followers

options.name: Fan-out on read (pull)
options.how: At read time, fetch the latest posts of each followee and merge them.
pros: No write amplification
Always fresh
cons: Hundreds of reads per feed request at ~70 k/s
p99 dominated by the slowest shard

options.name: Hybrid
options.how: Push for normal accounts; for accounts above ~100 k followers, followers pull their posts at read time and merge.
pros: Bounded write cost per post
Read merges only a handful of celebrity lists, which are themselves hot in cache
cons: Two paths to keep consistent
Threshold needs tuning and accounts crossing it need migration

deepDives.choice:
Hybrid. With an average of 200 followers, push costs ~116 k inserts/s, which a Redis cluster handles. The long tail of huge accounts is what breaks it, and a typical user follows only a few of those, so merging their recent posts at read time is cheap. Those posts sit in a small, very hot cache.

Two refinements: skip push for users inactive for 30 days and rebuild their timeline on next login, and run fan-out on a separate queue so a slow celebrity job never blocks normal posts. If the product moved to a ranked feed, the timeline would become a candidate pool of ~1 000 IDs and a ranker would pick from it.

diagram.title: Hybrid feed read
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as App
  participant F as Feed service
  participant T as Timeline cache
  participant C as Celebrity posts cache
  participant P as Post cache
  A->>F: GET feed with cursor
  F->>T: top 20 IDs below cursor
  F->>C: recent posts of followed big accounts
  F->>F: merge by time, take 20
  F->>P: multi-get post details
  F-->>A: page and nextCursor

deepDives.title: Like counts on viral posts
deepDives.problem: A viral post can get 50 k likes per second. Incrementing one counter row 50 k times a second makes a single hot key on a single node, and every feed render reads that count.

options.name: UPDATE count = count + 1 per like
options.how: Increment a column on the post row in the same request.
pros: Exact and simple
cons: Row lock contention on hot posts
Couples the like path to the posts database

options.name: Sharded counter
options.how: Split the counter into N sub-counters; each like increments a random one; reads sum them.
pros: Spreads write load N ways
Still near real time
cons: Reads must sum N keys
N must be chosen up front or grown dynamically

options.name: Event stream plus batched apply
options.how: Likes emit +1/-1 events partitioned by postId; a consumer sums per post per second and applies one increment.
pros: One write per post per second, whatever the like rate
Count store is decoupled from the like rows
cons: Count lags by about a second
Needs idempotent apply (track consumer offsets with the count)

deepDives.choice: Event stream plus batched apply. A post getting 50 k likes/s becomes one counter write per second. The source of truth is still the Like rows, so a nightly job can recount any post whose counter drifted. The app shows the user's own like optimistically, which satisfies 'I always see my own like'. If product needed exact live counts on stage for an event, a sharded counter for that one post would be the add-on.

failures: Image worker backlog grows (a bad deploy or a spike)
Posts stay in processing; the app shows the local copy to the author. Autoscale workers on queue lag; feed hides processing posts rather than showing broken images.
Replica takes over; if both are gone, rebuild affected timelines on read by pulling from followees for one request, then repopulate in the background.
A celebrity posts and fan-out would be millions of writes
Not pushed at all: followers pull it at read time. The threshold is enforced in the fan-out worker, not just by convention.
CDN or one edge region degrades
Multi-CDN with DNS steering; origin shield in front of object storage so a mass cache miss does not hit the bucket directly.
Profile pages for authors on that shard fail; the feed still serves IDs from the timeline and post details from the post cache. Writes for that shard queue and retry.
Duplicate post from a retried create call
Idempotency-Key stored with the post for 24 h; the second call returns the first post's ID.
scale: 10× users: image egress approaches 2 Tbps, so negotiate CDN capacity and add AVIF to cut bytes ~20%. Timeline cache grows to ~16 TB; keep timelines only for users active in the last 30 days.
Storage cost: at ~44 PB/year, move originals older than 90 days to an archive class and keep derived sizes hot. Deduplicate identical re-uploads by content hash.
Global users: keep object storage replicated to 2–3 regions, serve feeds from the nearest region with async replication of posts and follows, and accept seconds of cross-region feed lag.

followups.q: How do you stop the feed from showing a post whose images are not ready yet?
answer: Fan-out runs on PostCreated, but feed hydration filters status != ready.
Alternatively, fan out on PostReady instead of PostCreated; that adds ~1 s of delay but no filtering.
The author's own profile shows the post immediately using the local image.

followups.q: A user follows someone new. When do that person's posts show up?
answer: Follow triggers a backfill job that inserts the followee's last ~20 posts into the follower's timeline.
Until it runs, nothing breaks; the feed is just missing those posts for a few seconds.
Unfollow removes the followee's IDs lazily: the feed filters out authors no longer followed.

followups.q: How do you delete a post everywhere?
answer: Mark the post removed; feed hydration drops it, so timelines need no cleanup.
Delete derived files and purge the CDN paths; the original is deleted after a 30-day grace period for appeals.
Object keys include the postId, so the purge is a prefix purge.

followups.q: How would you add a ranked feed?
answer: Keep the timeline as a candidate pool of ~1 000 recent IDs instead of the final order.
A ranking service scores candidates with features like author affinity and engagement, under a ~50 ms budget.
Cache the ranked page per user for a few minutes so scrolling back up does not reshuffle.

followups.q: How do you keep EXIF GPS data from leaking home addresses?
answer: The image worker strips location metadata from every derived file.
Originals are never served publicly, only derived sizes.
Read access to originals is limited to the processing service and is logged.

mistakes: Streaming photo bytes through the application servers instead of using presigned uploads and a CDN.
Choosing pure fan-out on write and never mentioning accounts with millions of followers.
Storing images in the database as BLOBs.
Ignoring that originals are most of the storage cost and never discussing storage classes.
Incrementing a single like counter row per like and not noticing the hot key.

mid: Asked about video, feed ordering and celebrity accounts before drawing anything
Estimated storage per day and image egress, and concluded a CDN is required
Separated metadata (database) from image bytes (object storage)
Defined a cursor-paginated feed endpoint, not offset-based
Generated multiple image sizes rather than serving originals
senior: Used presigned direct uploads and explained why bytes stay off app servers
Made image processing async with a status field and explained what the author sees meanwhile
Chose hybrid fan-out with a stated follower threshold and justified it with the fan-out arithmetic
Handled hot like counters with batching or sharding and kept the like rows as source of truth
Named what happens when the timeline cache is lost and how it is rebuilt
staff: Proposed storage-class tiering for originals backed by the ~44 PB/year number
Discussed deletion end to end: feed filtering, CDN purge and retention of originals
Covered multi-region reads with async replication and stated the lag users accept
Raised privacy risks such as EXIF location and access control on originals
